title: ACS 65+ Broadband Subscription Share, 2025
question: U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey 2025 ACS 1-Year Estimates Detailed Table B28005, population 65 years and over in households with a computer and a broadband Internet subscription divided by total population 65 years and over in households, first print, percent.
resolutionSource: U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey 1-Year Estimates Detailed Table B28005. CRITICAL VINTAGE DISCIPLINE: base rates MUST come from ACS 1-YEAR estimates (ACSDT1Y products) for each history year, never 5-year (ACSDT5Y) tables — 5-year values lag the 1-year series by roughly two years and have corrupted prior runs of this target. Fetch per-year values keylessly from https://data.census.gov/api/access/data/table?id=ACSDT1Y{YEAR}.B28005&g=010XX00US and compute 100*B28005_017E/B28005_014E. Keep the published question text exactly: U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey 2025 ACS 1-Year Estimates Detailed Table B28005, population 65 years and over in households with a computer and a broadband Internet subscription divided by total population 65 years and over in households, first print, percent.
resolutionRule: Resolve to 100 * B28005_017E / B28005_014E for geography United States in the first public 2025 ACS 1-Year Estimates Detailed Table B28005 print, rounded to one decimal percentage point. Use the original Census first-posted estimate and ignore later revisions or corrections unless Census replaces the first public file before the public release completes.
drivers: Broadband definition includes cellular data, satellite, fixed wireless, and other non-dial-up service
Adoption gains should slow as the remaining offline 65+ population is more selected
Affordable Connectivity Program expiration creates affordability drag for low-income older households
ACS first-print sampling and weighting noise can move this national age subgroup around one percentage point

reasoning.text: Base rate/reference class: the best reference class is the same U.S. ACS 1-year B28005 age-65-plus series, which rose from 79.4 percent in 2021 to 84.8 percent in 2024. The 2024 all-household broadband measure at 91.0 percent is an upper-adoption context, while the 8.7 percent 65+ no-computer measure constrains how fast the B28005 broadband share can close the remaining gap.

Level, momentum, one-off, and mechanism: level starts from the 2024 same-series first-print value of 84.8 percent. Momentum is positive because each entering 65-year-old cohort is more connected than the oldest cohorts leaving the population, and the broadband category includes cellular data plans. One-off BEAD deployment effects are limited by timing because many funded projects will not materially change 2025 ACS collection-year subscriptions. ACP expiration before 2025 adds affordability drag for some low-income older households.

Prior/update/interval: persistence prior is the latest same-series 2024 U.S. ACS 1-year B28005 share of 84.8 percent. Historical sample is the same-series annual changes 2021-2022: 81.6 - 79.4 = +2.2, 2022-2023: 83.5 - 81.6 = +1.9, and 2023-2024: 84.8 - 83.5 = +1.3 percentage points, giving sigma = sqrt((2.2^2 + 1.9^2 + 1.3^2) / 3) = 1.8 percentage points as an annual-change RMS uncertainty proxy. Mechanism update adds +1.4 points for cohort replacement and continued mobile/fixed-wireless subscription diffusion, minus 0.2 for affordability drag and saturation, yielding point 86.0. The 80% half-width is about 1.28*sigma = 1.28*1.8 = 2.3, rounded to 2.4 for first-print sampling and table-noise risk, so bounds are 86.0 - 2.4 = 83.6 and 86.0 + 2.4 = 88.4.

Counter-considerations: upside risk is a stronger-than-expected jump in cellular-data-plan reporting or older-adult smartphone adoption, which would land above the interval if the 2025 share exceeds 88.4 percent. Downside risk is affordability churn after subsidy expiration, survey-composition noise, or a stall among the oldest and lowest-income households, which would land below the interval if the first print is under 83.6 percent. An outside the interval result would most likely reflect either a definitional/table change or a large one-year ACS sampling/weighting move rather than ordinary trend continuation.

Prior run update: a prior Thesis run for this target had the same point and interval after using the same public Census-derived 1-year B28005 history; I used it only as public provenance for official fetched counts after direct keyless API access failed in this environment, and not as ground-truth outcome evidence.
